query: For steels used in chemical-processing and nuclear-power applications, what testable mechanistic hypothesis could explain their resistance to corrosion? Specify a controlled study capable of revealing the governing cause, predicted observations relative to a baseline, the boundaries within which the hypothesis should hold, supporting evidence from prior findings, and a result that would falsify it.

generation.hypothesis: The corrosion resistance of steels used in chemical-processing and nuclear-power applications is governed by the in situ formation of a duplex oxide scale—an outer, continuous, and dense Al2O3 film coupled with an inner Cr-rich oxide layer—that together reduce oxygen ingress and metal dissolution by limiting ionic diffusion.
generation.material_initial_state: Standard ferritic/martensitic or ODS steels (e.g., T91 or 9Cr type) exhibiting conventional alloy compositions with low Al additions and typical grain structures.
generation.intervention: Modify the alloy composition by introducing a controlled amount of Al (and possibly minor Si) to promote the preferential formation of Al2O3 during high-temperature exposure.
generation.conditions: Exposure under high-temperature corrosive environments (e.g., liquid lead or lead–bismuth eutectic) at approximately 550–700 °C with a controlled, low-to-moderate oxygen content.
generation.structural_mediator: The formation of a duplex oxide layer consisting of an outer, adherent, dense Al2O3 film and an inner Cr-rich oxidation zone.
generation.mechanism: Due to its very high oxygen affinity and lower oxide formation free energy, Al oxidizes readily even under low oxygen partial pressures to form a stable and protective Al2O3 layer. This layer, in tandem with an internally formed Cr-rich oxide band, acts as a barrier to both oxygen ingress and outward metal ion diffusion (especially Fe, Cr, and others), thereby mitigating dissolution corrosion. The duplex layer limits the diffusion processes that are central to the corrosion mechanism in these high-temperatures, liquid metal environments.
generation.predicted_outcome: Steels modified with increased Al concentration should exhibit thinner overall corrosion depths, more uniform and adherent oxide films, and higher electrochemical resistance compared to baseline steels without the modification when subjected to corrosive high-temperature conditions.
generation.baseline: Steels with lower Al content that form a less continuous or more defective oxide layer, resulting in thicker, heterogeneous oxide scales and higher rates of corrosion penetration under identical conditions.
generation.boundary: This mechanism is assumed to hold in high-temperature, controlled-oxygen environments typical of liquid lead or LBE applications (roughly 550–700 °C). Its validity may not extend to low-temperature or highly variable oxygen conditions, and interactions with other elements (e.g., Si) or effects due to grain refinement may also modulate the outcome.
generation.uncertainty: There remains uncertainty regarding the optimum Al concentration needed to achieve the ideal duplex oxide structure and how additional alloying elements or microstructural variations (e.g., fine versus coarse grains) might quantitatively affect the protective behavior.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of steel samples with nearly identical microstructures and processing histories. One set will be the baseline steel with conventional low Al content, and the other will have a controlled higher Al addition designed to promote Al2O3 formation. Expose both sets to a liquid lead or lead–bismuth eutectic environment at approximately 600 °C under controlled oxygen levels for a fixed period (e.g., 1000 hours).
measurements: Measure corrosion penetration depth and oxide scale thickness via cross-sectional SEM/EDS analysis.
Perform electrochemical impedance spectroscopy to assess the resistance of the surface films.
Characterize the uniformity and phase composition of the oxide layers using XRD and TEM.
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the Al-enriched steels do not show a statistically significant reduction in corrosion penetration depth, form a more uniform/dense oxide film, and exhibit higher impedance (indicating better barrier properties) relative to the baseline steels, then the hypothesis that duplex oxide scale formation (mediated by Al addition) governs the improved corrosion resistance is falsified.

Compared with other corrosive media, such as high-temperature water or gas, the liquid metal in lead-based reactors has serious dissolution corrosion to structural materials at high temperature, especially the elements of Ni and Cr []. The T91 ferritic/martensitic steel does not contain Ni and has a lower content of Cr compared to austenitic steels and, therefore, is considered an important candidate for lead-cooled reactors. However, the working temperature of traditional ferritic/martensitic steel is usually below 550–600 °C, which cannot meet the service requirements of the future lead-cooled reactor. If introducing very fine oxide particles with a high number density into the matrix of steel, the operation temperature can be increased to 700 °C []. A thin local distributed layer with a thickness of 1 micron can be found along the original boundary, which separated the corrosion layer and Pb attached to the surface of the sample. EDS results show that this layer was rich in Cr and O elements, and the distribution of Cr and O is consistent, indicating that it was an oxide film rich in Cr2O3. However, this film is not continuous and dense enough due to the low Cr content of the material; therefore, it cannot play a protective role for the long-term corrosion resistance. As a result, there is white Pb under this layer, and there is an IOZ region at the boundary between the penetrated Pb and the matrix, which is a discontinuous internal oxidation product rich in Cr. This is consistent with the reported results of 9Cr ODS steel in flowing LBE. Under the condition of 10−6 wt% oxygen concentration, IOZ internal oxidation was always formed []. The corrosion behavior of T91, 9Cr ODS, and 9CrAl ODS in liquid Pb was tested and compared after exposure up to 2000 h at 600 °C. The main conclusions obtained are as follows: The surface color and luster of the different corrode materials were quite different. The color of T91 is abundant with a metallic luster due to the formation of complex oxidation products and attached lead. Most of the surface of 9Cr ODS is gray-white with a metallic luster due to the covered metallic lead. The color of the 9CrAl surface is quite uniform without metallic luster; The corrosion of 9Cr ODS is slightly heavier than that of T91 after corrosion for 1000 h. An oxide layer that grows outward is locally formed outside of T91, which plays a certain positive role in corrosion resistance, while the fine-grained structure of ODS steel promotes the accelerated dissolution of Fe and Cr, resulting in a lower rate of formation of oxidation products; The maximum corrosion depth of 9CrAl ODS is 51.8 μm after corrosion for 2000 h, which is much lower than that of 9Cr-ODS steel.
